newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Crime dampens SAfrica private construction - survey.
newsitem.headline: Crime dampens SAfrica private construction - survey.

text.p: South African privately financed construction activities fell more than 20 percent in 1992-1995 amid high crime rates, low levels of investment confidence and economic growth, a research study said.
The University of South Africa's Bureau for Market Research (BMR) said on Monday buildings completed by the private sector declined by 21.1 percent between 1992 and 1995.

It said the decline was particularly severe in non-residential buildings, which includes office, shopping and industrial space, with the real value of economic space completed shrinking 55 percent to 1.2 billion in 1995 from to 2.1 billion rand in 1992.
Although privately financed residential buildings in 1995 stayed steady at its 1992 level of 3.3 billion rand, it fell far short of reconstruction and development programme (RDP) targets.

It said the RDP had hoped in 1995 to increase housing delivery to 300,000 units a year. But the total number of residential units completed by the private sector from 1992 to 1995 amounted to under 150,000. This figure, however, did not include government-financed building activities.
The BMR said the increased crime rate had caused considerable changes in the type of residential units completed by the private sector since 1992.
Townhouses, with their higher security features, increased their share in the value of residential buildings completed to 25.9 percent in 1995 from 15.2 percent in 1992.
In provincial breakdowns, all provinces except for Gauteng and the Western Cape, showed a reverse discrepancy between their shares in building construction and population, the BMR said.
Because construction activities by the private sector were indicative of economic prospects, creating an environment conducive to new investment was seen as key for future growth.
"Crime prevention and a consistent macro-economic framework are two of the most important prerequisites for future investment," the BMR said.
